name: deark
desc: File conversion utility for older formats
why: Extracts and converts obscure legacy file formats, a rewarding dive into forgotten binary structures.

brief.what_it_is: Deark is a free, open-source, portable command-line utility that decodes certain older or obscure file formats. It either converts them to a more modern or more readable format, or extracts embedded files from them. It can also print detailed technical information about a file's contents and metadata with -d. Input is a legacy file such as an image, icon, font, archive, disk image, or executable-packed file. Output is usually written as files named output.* (or into a ZIP or TAR archive with -zip or -tar).
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to turn files in forgotten or obsolete formats into something modern or readable, and to pull embedded files out of them. The author also notes that Deark contains a lot of knowledge about third-party formats (structures, algorithms, tables, palettes) that is otherwise scattered.
brief.how_it_works: Deark autodetects the format of the input file and hands it to a format-specific module; -m selects a module by hand when detection fails or a special-purpose module like copy is wanted. Each module decodes the format and writes the converted or extracted items as output files, with many options controlling names, timestamps, and containers. The README notes that archive formats are best converted to ZIP with -zip -ka so filenames and paths are kept. The formats.txt file lists the modules.

brief.install_notes: The homepage offers a source tarball (deark-1.7.3.tar.gz) and a Windows 64-bit x64 binary in an x64 directory. Windows users may need a tool that handles .tar.gz, such as 7-Zip. Build instructions are in technical.md, which I did not open. No account, runtime, or configuration is mentioned. Beyond brew install, I saw no first-run steps.
brief.standout: Deark is one tool covering a very wide spread of legacy formats, including ANSI art, DOS executable packers, Macintosh resource forks, Palm OS, EPOC/Symbian, and calculator pictures. It also has a debug-style inspection mode (-d) that dumps a file's internal structure. Options also let you cap output size, restrict modules for security workflows (-onlymods, -disablemods), and make archive output reproducible.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists a release, deark-1.7.3.tar.gz, dated 2026-06-10. The README says feature lists are as of 2025-09, and the copyright runs through 2026. I did not see a commit history.
brief.caveats: The README warns that features are subject to change without notice. Unrecognized or misspelled -opt options are silently ignored. Images larger than 10000 pixels in either dimension are refused by default, and large images are not generated efficiently. A malformed input usually produces an error message but exit status 0. The README says it is not really a collaborative project and that unsolicited contributions of more than a few lines are unlikely to be accepted. The main code is MIT-style licensed, but files in the foreign subdirectory have their own terms. Windows users need a .tar.gz-capable tool. The -modcodes option is mainly for developers.
quotes: Deark is a portable command-line utility that can decode certain types of files, and either convert them to a more-modern or more-readable format, or extract embedded files from them.
Caution: Unrecognized or misspelled options will be silently ignored.
